summary: Provides guidelines for evaluating the performance of IPv6 transition technologies that use encapsulation or translation. Dual-stack nodes can be tested using RFCs 2544 and 5180. It also includes a metric for load scalability.

plainLanguage.summary: A fair test that measures how well the tools for moving from old to new internet addresses perform.

questions: how to benchmark ipv6 transition technologies
dual dut vs single dut test setup
subtitle: How to benchmark IPv6 transition gear that translates or encapsulates, extending RFC 2544 and RFC 5180.

tldr.problem: Existing benchmarking methods cover IPv4 and IPv6 devices, but not IPv6 transition technologies that translate or encapsulate packets between the two.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the RFC 2544 tests where it can, adds new procedures for latency, packet delay variation, DNS64 performance and overload scalability, and defines single and dual device-under-test setups.
tldr.outcome: It gives vendors and operators a common way to compare translation and encapsulation technologies. It is Informational, and nothing in the unit metadata says it has been replaced.

today: RFC 8219 is an Informational RFC published in August 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Transition Technologies Need Their Own Benchmarks
sections.content:
RFC 2544 and RFC 5180 help analyze IPv4 and IPv6 capable network devices, but RFC 5180 does not cover IPv6 transition technologies. IPv6 is not backwards compatible, so IPv4-only nodes cannot talk directly to IPv6-only nodes, and transition technologies exist to bridge that gap.

RFC 8219 therefore gives benchmarking guidelines for them. It also adds an approach to measure overload scalability: how gracefully a device copes with more flows than the maximum it can operate normally.
sections.plainLanguage: Old tests could time normal roads. This one times the special bridges that connect the old road system to the new one.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Transition Technology
sections.content:
The RFC pictures a network as Domain A, a core domain and Domain B, with IPvX and IPvY standing for IPv4 and IPv6 (X is not equal to Y). Technologies are grouped by how they cross the core domain.

  • Dual stack: core devices speak both protocols. RFC 2544 and RFC 5180 are enough to test it.
  • Single translation: IPvX packets are translated to IPvY at the edge of Domain A. Examples listed are NAT64 and IVI.
  • Double translation: packets are translated at both edges. Examples listed are 464XLAT and MAP-T.
  • Encapsulation: packets are wrapped in IPvY and unwrapped at the far edge. Examples listed are DS-Lite, MAP-E, Lightweight 4over6, 6rd, 6PE and 6VPE.

The RFC also separates stateful technologies, which keep a state table of address mappings (for example Stateful NAT64), from stateless ones. Extra tests are RECOMMENDED for the stateful kind.
sections.plainLanguage: You can skip the bridge, swap the language once, swap it twice, or put a letter inside another envelope. Each trick needs its own test.

sections.title: Test Setups and Test Traffic
sections.content:
For single translation, a single DUT setup SHOULD be used, with the Tester supporting both IPvX and IPvY. For encapsulation and double translation, a dual DUT setup SHOULD be used: the first DUT converts IPvX to IPvY and the second converts it back. Because a dual setup cannot show asymmetries between the two devices, extra tests SHOULD use the single DUT setup.

Tests SHOULD use bidirectional UDP traffic, because UDP measurements give a more reliable basis for comparison. The recommended mixes are IPvX only, 90% IPvX with 10% native IPvY, 50% and 50%, and 10% IPvX with 90% IPvY. The frame sizes for Ethernet are 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1518, 1522, 2048, 4096, 8192 and 9216 bytes. Encapsulation or translation overhead MUST be taken into account, and the RECOMMENDED MTU is the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 bytes plus that overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: You send the same test cars through one translator booth, or through a pair of booths, and you must remember that translating changes the size of the car.

sections.title: The Benchmarking Tests
sections.content:
Throughput, frame loss rate, back-to-back frames and system recovery reuse the RFC 2544 sections unmodified, and reset reuses RFC 6201. The new procedures are these.

  • Latency: send a stream of at least 120 seconds at the throughput rate and tag at least 500 frames after 60 seconds. Report the median as typical latency and the 99.9th percentile as worst-case latency, repeating the test at least 20 times.
  • Packet delay variation (PDV): RECOMMENDED. It is the 99.9th percentile of one-way delay minus the minimum delay, over a stream of at least 60 seconds. Inter packet delay variation (IPDV) MAY be added for fine-grained analysis.
  • Stateful extras: concurrent TCP connection capacity and maximum TCP connection establishment rate, both taken unmodified from RFC 3511.

Every result is repeated at least 20 times and summarized with the median plus the 1st and 99th percentiles, so a single number does not over-summarize.
sections.plainLanguage: You time many cars many times, then report the typical time and the slowest time, not just one lucky run.

sections.title: DNS64 and Overload Scalability
sections.content:
DNS64 is the DNS support used with single-translation technologies such as NAT64. The Tester acts as both client and authoritative DNS server. It sends AAAA queries to the DUT, and the DUT asks for the AAAA record, gets an empty answer, asks for the A record and returns a synthesized AAAA record. The test finds the highest rate of queries per second for which every reply arrives within a timeout that defaults to 1 second. Trials SHOULD last at least 60 seconds. The required baseline uses 0% cached names and 0% names with AAAA records; other mixes are OPTIONAL.

Overload scalability is measured by running the Section 7 tests with one flow and then with n flows, and computing the relative change. For lower-is-better metrics such as latency the degradation is (Xn - X1) / X1 * 100. For higher-is-better metrics such as throughput it is (X1 - Xn) / X1 * 100. Flows can start all at once or one after another at interval t.
sections.plainLanguage: One test asks a phone book helper to translate names as fast as it can. Another sees how much slower things get when many people use the bridge at once.

sections.title: Security and Addressing Notes
sections.content:
Benchmarking is limited to characterization with controlled stimuli in a laboratory with dedicated address space. The test topology MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network. Testing is black-box, and special benchmarking-only capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the DUT.

No IANA action is requested. The prefix 2001:2::/48 is already allocated for IPv6 benchmarking and 198.18.0.0/15 is reserved for IPv4 benchmarking.
sections.plainLanguage: Test in a closed practice yard, never on the real road, and do not give the car special tricks just for the test.
